MethodChannel.invokeMethod cannot invoke async native method

### Steps to reproduce

On Flutter, MethodChannel.invokeMethod is an async function. However, in Android Java code, MethodCallHandler.onMethodCall is a *synchronous* method, and this method does not accept a callback function that can be used to asynchronously pass the result back to Dart.

This is a problem when the API you are calling is asynchronous, or when you have to do a lot of work on the Java side (because onMethodCall is run on the UI thread, so you end up blocking the UI thread).

For a good example of why supporting the asynchronous case is important, see the Android Geocoder [URL] docs:

> **Warning:** This API may hit the network, and may block for excessive amounts of time, up to 60 seconds or more. It's strongly encouraged to use the asynchronous version of this API. If that is not possible, this should be run on a background thread to avoid blocking other operations.

For this API, the synchronous/blocking calls have the form:

[CODE]

and the asynchronous calls have the form:

[CODE]

However, there is no way for onMethodCall to defer sending back the result until the Geocoder.GeocodeListener is called.

I assume the "correct" way to do this currently is to use an EventChannel for the return values. However, that then detaches the response from the request.

### Expected results

Async Java calls should work with MethodChannel.

The Dart side is already making an async call, so only the Java side needs to be modified to support async calls.

Maybe there could to be another onMethodCall method added to MethodCallHandler that takes a callback parameter, and that would be called preferentially over the synchronous version.

### Actual results

Only synchronous calls may be made currently by onMethodCall.

path_provider_win/linux should support Dart-only use cases

### Use case

path_provider_windows and path_provider_linux both use FFI bindings and Dart-only code for determining the locations of relevant paths. However, they both take a dependency on Flutter, which prevents these packages from being used in a Dart-only context (e.g. in a Dart CLI).

Currently, I've just copy/pasted the code into my CLI and removed the Flutter dependency bits. But it would be great if these packages did not depend on Flutter so that they could be used directly in these cases.

### Proposal

Currently, path_provider_linux and path_provider_windows only use the Flutter SDK for @visibleForTesting, which could be consumed from package:meta instead. Transitively, though, they both depend on Flutter via path_provider_platform_interface which holds the MethodChannel implementation.

However, since the Android and iOS implementations have been migrated to Pigeon, it seems like this interface is no longer needed, and even path_provider_platform_interface could be migrated to no longer take a dependency on the Flutter SDK.

Ignore duplicate FlutterView.render calls in the same frame

### Background

Currently the FlutterView.render calls are "batched": the UI thread collects all rendered scenes and submits them to the raster thread once the frame ends. In other words, the raster thread does not start rasterization until the UI thread has received all scenes.

In the future, we would like to be able to "stream" renders: the UI thread sends each rendered scene to the raster thread as it receives them. This would allow the UI and raster threads to work in parallel on the same frame.

### Problem

What happens if I render a view multiple times in the same frame with different scenes? These re-renders should be ignored to ensure that the raster thread does not have to do throwaway work in a "streaming" world.

- If set to false, no vibration should occur in any case

[Impeller] AHB sampled textures use nearest sampling instead of linear.

This differs from the GL backend where sampling is linear. See the difference between the two (ignore the rotation, thats just an artifact of me not applying the patch to migrate to SurfaceProducer cleanly [URL]). This is because we don't enable separate reconstruction filters when sampling [URL] and don't check for linear sampling support [URL] when creating the conversion.

### SurfaceTexture
[IMAGE]

### SurfaceProducer
[IMAGE]

[Impeller] Allow both linear and nearest sampling of AHB backed Vulkan textures.

Today, AHB backed textures will prefer linear sampling (after checking for VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_SAMPLED_IMAGE_YCBCR_CONVERSION_LINEAR_FILTER_BIT) and fallback to nearest sampling. That is, sampling will ignore the min and mag filter specified in the impeller::SamplerDescriptor. This is because of stricter requirements when sampling from AHBs.

If VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_SAMPLED_IMAGE_YCBCR_CONVERSION_LINEAR_FILTER_BIT is not supported, there is no way linear sample without a render to an intermediate texture.

On the other hand, if VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_SAMPLED_IMAGE_YCBCR_CONVERSION_LINEAR_FILTER_BIT is supported, using nearest sampling is not possible today because we create only a single conversion.

It may be tempting to just check for VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_SAMPLED_IMAGE_YCBCR_CONVERSION_SEPARATE_RECONSTRUCTION_FILTER_BIT and use whatever is specified in the impeller::SamplerDescriptor. While this is extremely convenient, in practice, this bit is never set on most Android formats.

To work around this, a completely separate conversion must be created and cached in the conversions library. And, in the relatively uncommon case where linear sampling is not supported, a separate render to texture must be performed.

This describes an edge case since most uses require linear sampling and that seems to be well supported out of the box. But, if we get reports of users depending on specific kinds of sampling, we should look into using separate conversions and (in extreme cases to catch lack of support for direct linear sampling) render to texture.

### Use case

Currently, there isn't a way to choose when the zoom-based clustering happens via the new cluster feature for Google Maps. Custom clustering at multiple zoom levels is essential for location-based applications.

Video Ad Midroll And Postroll

### Use case

How we can rerquest ad again when playing video (Midroll)

Midroll Ads
Midroll ads are video advertisements that appear in the middle of video content.

Postroll Ads
Postroll ads, on the other hand, appear at the end of video content.

### Proposal

**Midroll Ads**
Midroll ads are video advertisements that appear in the middle of video content. They are commonly used in longer videos or live streaming content and typically play after a specific time interval. The purpose of midroll ads is to engage viewers at a point when they are already invested in the content, which can lead to higher completion rates and better ad recall. For instance, on platforms like YouTube, midroll ads may play every 10-15 minutes in a video over 10 minutes long, breaking up the content similarly to traditional commercial breaks on television.

Benefits of Midroll Ads:
Higher engagement: Viewers are less likely to skip these ads as they are already engrossed in the content.
Longer ad durations possible: Since they appear mid-content, midroll ads can be slightly longer without risking a high drop-off rate.
More natural integration: They mimic traditional TV ad breaks, making them more familiar to viewers.
Challenges of Midroll Ads:
Viewer disruption: Some viewers may find these ads intrusive as they interrupt the video experience.
Content pacing issues: If not strategically placed, midroll ads can break the flow of the content, potentially diminishing viewer experience.

**Postroll Ads**
Postroll ads, on the other hand, appear at the end of video content. They play once the main content has concluded, usually when viewers are wrapping up their viewing experience. While postroll ads may not always receive the same level of attention as pre-roll or midroll ads, they can be effective for certain types of messaging—especially calls to action (CTAs) like visiting a website, subscribing, or checking out related content.

Benefits of Postroll Ads:
Non-intrusive: Postroll ads do not interrupt the viewing experience, as they appear once the content has ended.
Ideal for CTAs: Since viewers may be looking for what to do next, postroll ads are good for prompts such as directing traffic to additional content or other channels.
Better for brand-friendly campaigns: Since the viewer has voluntarily finished the content, there’s often a positive association that can carry over into the ad.
Challenges of Postroll Ads:
Lower viewability: Viewers may choose to stop the video before the postroll ad begins, resulting in lower engagement rates.
Limited attention: Since postroll ads come after the main content, viewer attention can be lower, which might reduce the effectiveness of branding or storytelling campaigns.

SurfaceProducer needs a "will destroy" signal, not a "did destroy"

This is the same issue as #152839.

To recap, the SurfaceProducer API currently provides an onSurfaceDestroyed callback that is invoked after a surface has been destroyed. However, if the surface is being accessed by another thread, this is too late to do any cleanup as the thread may attempt to access the surface in between the call to cleanup() and the callback being invoked. Instead, we need a callback that is invoked *before* the call to cleanup() so that the rendering thread can be notified appropriately.

[CODE]

This is the reason for the video_player package needing to destroy and recreate the entire player instance, as ExoPlayer will attempt to access the surface from the renderer thread after it has been destroyed, and go into an invalid state. This workaround is problematic as it breaks background playback, and results in the entire player state needing to be reloaded. This [URL] comment in the previous issue mentioned that it impossible to avoid this save/restore of the state, but this is not true since an onSurfaceDestroying callback would allow us to call player.setVideoSurface(null) on the ExoPlayer instance to ensure that it does not access the surface once it is destroyed, and allow playback to continue without a video surface.

Request to Support Overriding libapp.so on Android | To Enable Custom Code Push Feature

Hi Flutter Team,

We are considering implementing a code-push-like feature for our Flutter Android app, similar to how react-native-code-push operates. After reviewing the Flutter Engine codebase, specifically this file: FlutterLoader.java [URL], we believe that supporting the ability to override FlutterApplicationInfo.aotSharedLibraryName at runtime would make it possible for us, or the community, to build a similar feature.

## How will we implement code push?

In a standard Flutter release APK, the app loads libapp.so by default. When a new patch is available, our custom implementation would download a new shared library (e.g., libapp-arm64-v1.0.1.so) specific to the device. The next time the app opens, we would use the downloaded libapp-*.so file, applying the patch. We could manage the correct library version to use by storing it in SharedPreferences or a similar local storage solution.

## Why not use existing solutions?

1. Shorebird.dev: It's not fully open source,
2. Flutter RFW: Implementing code push like solution using RFW adds High maintenance, complexity.

Although we could maintain a fork of Flutter internally with these changes, it seems to be a small modification within a few files under the path engine/src/flutter/shell/platform/android/io/flutter/embedding/engine/loader/*

## Security considerations

1. **No Impact for Apps Without Overrides:** Apps that don't implement this override will not be affected; only those with the code-push implementation will see changes.
2. **Compatibility Check:** If the newly downloaded libapp-*.so is incompatible with the app’s native build, it won’t load. so a libapp.so patch intended for a 3rd person shooter game is not going to work in basic calculator app.
3. **Similar to React-Native Code Push**: This approach mirrors how react-native handles code updates by delivering new index.android.bundle files. In this case, we'd be delivering libapp-*.so files, a technique that’s been widely used in production apps.

## Questions:

1. What are your thoughts on this approach?
2. Is there an existing way to achieve this that we may have missed?

Thanks for the amazing framework! We look forward to hearing your thoughts.

New "Best Practices" Project Template as Skeleton Alternative

### Use case

When creating a new Flutter project, developers (especially newcomers) lack a starter template that demonstrates widely accepted best practices. The removal of the skeleton template has left a gap where projects default to the overly simplistic counter app, which doesn’t guide users on critical topics like internationalization, scalable architecture, routing, or testing. This forces developers to manually research and integrate these practices, leading to inconsistent setups, duplicated effort, and potential technical debt.

**Current Limitations**
- The default counter template focuses on basic functionality, not real-world app structure.
- Newcomers often reinvent the wheel or adopt outdated patterns due to lack of official guidance.
- Teams spend time rebuilding boilerplate for routing, state management, and localization instead of focusing on features.

### Proposal

Introduce a new **official project template** (e.g., flutter create --template best_practices) that serves as a foundation for production-ready apps. This template would:

1. **Demonstrate Best Practices**
- **Clean Architecture**: Separate layers (presentation, domain, data).
- **State Management**: Provider/Riverpod/Bloc setup with example.
- **Routing**: GoRouter/Navigator 2.0 with named routes and deep linking.
- **Internationalization**: Localization with ARB files.
- **Theming**: Light/dark mode, custom design system.
- **Testing**: Unit, widget, and integration test examples.

2. **Target Audience**
- **Newcomers**: Quick starting point to learn best practices.
- **Experienced Devs**: Save time of boilerplate setup.

3. **Minimal but Opinionated**
- Avoid overcomplication; focus on a structure that scales.
- Use flutter.dev [URL] recommended packages where possible (e.g., go_router for navigation).

**Why Flutter Should Provide This**
- **Ecosystem Health**: Reduces fragmentation by promoting consistent patterns.
- **Onboarding**: Lowers the barrier to entry for new Flutter developers.
- **Adoption**: A "batteries included" template makes Flutter more appealing for enterprise/production use.

iOS Document UX Support In-Situ Editing with Security Scoped URLs

### Use case

For a document editing Flutter application running on iPadOS there is no capability for a user to specify a document for editing in-situ. The document has to be copied into the app sandbox and then the user reminded to copy it back when done editing.

In an ideal word the user can select the document or directory that it wishes the app to edit documents in. iOS supports this capability natively, and Flutter does in all platforms except iOS.

The UIDocumentPickerViewController returns security scoped URLs that can be used to support direct IO with the referenced resource. Flutter file_picker currently copies the file into the sandbox rather than integrating the security scoped URLs.

As a result applications written in Flutter cannot provide a consistent UX across all platforms; the implementation cannot be cross-platform resulting in platform specific app codebases; and Flutter iOS apps provide a poor, complex UX requiring the user to share files back to where they came from once done editing.

### Proposal

Flutter File_Picker to integrate the security scoped URLs such that IO to them can be performed using regular dart APIs.

Automated reporting of crashes and ANRs from Google Play to Flutter libraries?

### Use case

I’ve noticed that tracking library-specific crashes in Flutter apps often requires manually digging through crash data in tools like the Google Play Console and then sharing it with library maintainers. It’s a tedious, copy-paste-heavy process that slows down debugging and improving libraries.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please give a clear and concise description of what the problem is.**

Yes! The problem is that crash reporting for libraries isn’t streamlined. Developers have to manually extract crash stats from app stores or tools and report them to library maintainers (e.g., via GitHub issues). This takes time, and key crash data might get missed or delayed, making it harder to fix issues fast.

**Describe the alternative solutions you've considered. Is there a package on pub.dev/flutter that already solves this?**

I’ve looked into existing solutions like Firebase Crashlytics, which is great for app-level crash reporting, but it doesn’t automatically isolate and share library-specific crashes with maintainers. There are packages on pub.dev for crash reporting (e.g., sentry or crashlytics), but none seem to offer an opt-in, automated way to report library crashes directly to a central hub like GitHub. Manual reporting is still the norm, which feels outdated when so much else is automated.

### Proposal

**Briefly but precisely describe what you would like Flutter to be able to do.**
I’d love for Flutter to support an opt-in feature where library crashes are automatically detected and reported, potentially by pulling data from sources like the Google Play Console. Imagine a setup where, with user consent, crash data linked to specific libraries (e.g., version X of package Y) is extracted from the Play Console (or other crash reporting tools) and sent to a central hub—like GitHub—for maintainers to analyze and act on quickly.

Write widgets in pure Flutter

### Use case

Flutter's goal is to be a cross-platform framework for mobile apps and to-date it's one of the best. However a major limitation of it is that you can't make cross-platform home screen widgets. As of now, you have to write them natively in kotlin/swift, and use a package to send data to the flutter app and vice versa.

It would be extremely useful to write some flutter code and have it rendered as a widget. I think the reason this wasn't done yet is due to the fact that the flutter rendering engine takes some time to start up, and android limitations on widgets so they don't consume battery life. However there is a simple way this can be done without the flutter rendering engine at all and follows all Android/ios restrictions on widgets.

### Proposal

This can be done extremely easily. The user writes the same Flutter code for the widget, then have a transpiler that converts it into valid Kotlin/swift that renders an identical-looking widget to what the user wrote in Flutter. Basically, the user writes dart and a transpiler converts it into kotlin/swift. The transpiler generates the same widget boilerplate that android/ios does, and then just changes the widget tree inside it to what the end user wrote in dart.

It doesn't have to be as advanced as the rendering system Flutter already has. Just something simple to write basic flutter graphics/widgets and pass some data into it.

I think this would be a massive improvement to Flutter and am surprised nobody's opened an issue like this up until now. It would be easy to implement and give Flutter a massive leg up compared to all other cross-platform frameworks.

4. Auto-completion
5. Error/warning indicators
6. Search and replace

3. Makes it difficult to build IDEs and development tools in Flutter
4. Creates inconsistent experiences across platforms

[Solved] GTK 3.0 development libraries are required for Linux development. [Ubuntu 24.04 with brew]

This is a post to save people's time.

Note: I'm not asking for help. I'm just reporting an issue that I had with flutter doctor. Issue [URL] is locked, so I'm writing here for future reference. This took me time to solve (even with ChatGPT).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Linux with brew present in the system;
2. Have pkg-config installed using brew;
2. Don´t have PKG_CONFIG_PATH set in ~/bashrc;
3. Run flutter doctor

Note: I use fvm.

## Problem

When running fvm flutter doctor -v

I was getting this:

✗ GTK 3.0 development libraries are required for Linux development.
They are likely available from your distribution (e.g.: apt install libgtk-3-dev)

## Diagnostic

Nothing was missing. I tried to fix the following Flutter Docs, and everything listed in the issue [URL] but I got no results.

Running the command pkg-config --cflags --libs gtk+-3.0 showed that some package was missing, but in reality was an issue in having pkg-config installed using brew along with the default (apt) pkg-config.

## Solution

There are two options:

1) brew uninstall pkg-config
But this is not an actual fix because in the future, this could recur when some brew command installs pkg-config again.

2) set PKG_CONFIG_PATHin the end of ~/bashrc to point to default (apt) package location
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pkgconfig:/usr/share/pkgconfig (your solution could be a different path)

By doing that The Flutter Doctor pass all tests

## Prognostic

The real question is that I'm not sure if this is only related to the way that flutter doctor checks if the packages are installed, or if having both brew and default pkg-config could impact Flutter Linux development. This is my first time with Flutter and Linux.

I know that using brew in Ubuntu is not optimal and could introduce conflicts, but tools are there to help, and people used to MacOS will be more likely to use brew for some things, right? We can´t control what other people are choosing, but we can advise them and help them learn. This is my contribution.

## What could you help with?

1. Check if having pkg-config in both apt and brew could result in problems in development or only with flutter doctor.
2. Document findings and see if the flutter doctor could be improved.

[go_router] Feature Request: Expose observers parameter for StatefulShellRoute to support RouteAware in nested navigators

StatefulShellRoute provides a way to implement tabbed navigation with preserved state for each branch (shell). However, I can't find a way to attach NavigatorObserver instances (like RouteObserver) specifically to the nested Navigator widget(s) it manages internally for its branches.

This is a problem when trying to use standard Flutter patterns like the RouteAware mixin on pages within a StatefulShellRoute branch. RouteAware relies on ModalRoute.of(context) to find its associated route and navigator, and then subscribes to a RouteObserver associated with that navigator.

If a RouteObserver is only added to the top-level GoRouter constructor's observers list, it only observes the root navigator. Navigation events happening within the StatefulShellRoute's nested navigator (e.g., pushing a detail page onto a branch's initial page) are not seen by the global observer. Consequently, RouteAware methods (didPush, didPop, didPopNext, didPushNext) do not get called for pages managed by the StatefulShellRoute's navigator.

**Example Scenario:**

1. App uses StatefulShellRoute for bottom navigation (e.g., Tabs A, B, C).
2. Tab A's initial route is /a.
3. From /a, the user navigates to /a/detail. The DetailPage uses RouteAware.
4. A global RouteObserver is added via GoRouter(observers: [myGlobalObserver]).
5. The DetailPage subscribes using myGlobalObserver.subscribe(this, ModalRoute.of(context)!).
6. Problem: The ModalRoute.of(context) correctly finds the route within the shell's navigator, but myGlobalObserver is not attached to that specific navigator, so the RouteAware callbacks on DetailPage never fire when navigating to/from it within Tab A.

### Proposed Solution:

Add an observers parameter to the StatefulShellRoute definition (and consequently to the TypedStatefulShellRoute annotation helper). This parameter would accept a List<NavigatorObserver>.

[CODE]

These observers would then be attached to the nested Navigator widget(s) created and managed by the StatefulShellRoute for its branches.

flutter command line causes cmd window to close on windows when git is missing

We've recently had quite a few people with installation problems over on the FlutterDev discord report that running any flutter command causes their cmd window to close. This, of course, only happens on Windows.

We narrowed it down to the fact that shared.bat uses the EXIT command without /B in several places, causing the entire cmd window to close. Seeing as this is often used immediately after reporting an error, this means users never get a chance to see the actual error message.

We've seen this from people trying to run flutter without Git in their path, or without PowerShell in their path, but there may be other cases that can trigger the issue.

This can be worked around by spawning another CMD shell within the existing CMD prompt, then running flutter inside that - which causes the nested CMD to exit, but the parent CMD remains so the error message is visible.

[video_player] Adopt FFI for most communication

We plan to use video_player as a production demonstration of a plugin developed with a hybrid of traditional Flutter plugin development and FFI on both Android and iOS/macOS. The general plan is:
- Reduce, but not eliminate, the amount of native code, by migrating more logic to Dart (in keeping with the overall trend of the flutter/plugin repository)
- The plugin system will continue to be used, especially for things like the texture system that we don't currently have a non-plugin replacement for.
- Use ffigen/jnigen to create bindings to the plugin code, and replace most method channel calls with FFI. In particular, the goal would be for all of the calls to individual player instances to be made via FFI.
- The switch to FFI for an implementation won't land until thread merging is non-optional on the target platform, as handling the thread hopping via FFI would add a lot of complexity. As a result, incremental refactoring will happen while still using method channels for everything, and then switching those out for FFI will be the last step.

The primary goal here is to ensure that we are consumers of this development model, as this hybrid approach would be likely incremental adoption model for the many existing plugins out there (including more of our own plugins in the future). Secondarily, this change will make it easier to avoid some of the state coordination problems this plugin suffers from, by making it easy to live-query native state instead of always trying to synchronize it. Severe Latency When Rendering Raw ui.Image from FFI on Android

I'm stuck at a major performance issue where there is a very large, unaccountable delay between when my application has fully decoded image data ready and when that image is actually rendered on screen.

To achieve the best possible performance, I have built a custom image pipeline using FFI to a native C++ thread pool. This architecture completely avoids Dart Isolates to eliminate all data-copying and serialization overhead between the main thread and the image processing code.

The data flow is as follows:
1. My C++ code loads a .qoi image file.
2. It decodes this file into a raw RGBA pixel buffer.
3. A pointer to this raw buffer is sent back to Dart via an FFI callback.
4. In Dart, I use ui.decodeImageFromPixels to upload these raw pixels to the GPU.
5. Finally, the resulting ui.Image is displayed using the RawImage widget.

I have instrumented every single step of this process. The native C++ work and the FFI communication are exceptionally fast. However, the total end-to-end time is an order of magnitude higher, suggesting a significant bottleneck within the Flutter framework itself.

### The Performance Data

The following metrics were captured on an Android 15 device, with timings being nearly identical in both profile and release modes.

**Explanation of Table Headers:**

* **Load Time:** The time spent in C++ purely on I/O (reading the file from disk).
* **Decode Time:** The time spent in C++ purely on CPU work (decoding the QOI file into raw RGBA pixels).
* **FFI Round-trip:** The total time from the Dart UI calling the loadImage function to the FFI callback arriving back in Dart with the raw pixel data. This measures the *entire* native process plus communication overhead.
* **GPU Upload:** The time taken by the ui.decodeImageFromPixels function to create a ui.Image (GPU texture) from the raw RGBA buffer.
* **End-to-End:** The total time from the UI requesting the image to it being rendered on screen, measured using a postFrameCallback.

**Performance Metrics (in Milliseconds):**

| Request # | Load Time | Decode Time | FFI Round-trip | GPU Upload | **End-to-End (Total)** |
| :-------- | :-------- | :---------- | :------------- | :--------- | :--------------------- |
| 0 | 0.404 | 3.957 | 5 | 6 | **273** |
| 1 | 0.217 | 3.318 | 6 | 4 | **274** |
| 8 | 0.205 | 7.154 | 11 | 5 | **438** |
| 9 | 0.139 | 2.710 | 4 | 3 | **445** |
| 26 | 0.136 | 2.672 | 4 | 1 | **88** |
| 27 | 0.119 | 2.443 | 4 | 1 | **87** |

The package:web version 1.1.1 fails to compile on Flutter 3.35.3 with Dart 3.9.2, throwing numerous JSObject, JSAny, and JSArray type errors, preventing Android builds from completing.

## Environment
- **Flutter Version**: 3.35.3 (stable channel)
- **Dart Version**: 3.9.2
- **Platform**: Windows 11, Android build target
- **package:web version**: 1.1.1
- **IDE**: VS Code with Flutter extension

## Error Description
When attempting to build for Android with flutter build apk --debug, the build fails with hundreds of type errors from the package:web library. The errors indicate that JSObject, JSAny, JSArray and related JS interop types are not recognized.

## Sample Errors
[CODE]

## Root Cause
The package:web 1.1.1 appears to have internal issues with dart:js_interop types not being properly available or exported, causing compilation failures even though the package itself declares compatibility with the Dart SDK version.

## Impact
This issue prevents any Flutter project that depends on package:web 1.1.1 (either directly or transitively) from building for Android. Many popular packages now require web ^1.1.0, including:
- device_info_plus ^11.5.0
- share_plus ^11.1.0
- file_picker ^10.3.1
- sentry_flutter ^9.6.0
- cloud_functions ^6.0.0
- flutter_image_compress ^2.4.0

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a new Flutter project with Flutter 3.35.3
2. Add web: ^1.1.0 to pubspec.yaml dependencies
3. Run flutter pub get
4. Run flutter build apk --debug
5. Observe compilation errors

## Expected Behavior
The package:web should compile successfully with Flutter 3.35.3 and Dart 3.9.2, as it claims compatibility with Dart SDK ">=3.4.0 <4.0.0".

## Actual Behavior
Compilation fails with numerous type errors related to JS interop types (JSObject, JSAny, JSArray, etc.) not being recognized.

## Attempted Workarounds
1. **Downgrading package:web**: Attempted to use version 1.0.0, but many dependencies now require ^1.1.0
2. **Downgrading dependencies**: Would require downgrading 6+ major packages, potentially breaking features
3. **Using exact version 1.1.0**: Still requires downgrading Firebase packages that need ^1.1.1

## Suggested Fix
The package:web library needs to properly export or make available the dart:js_interop types (JSObject, JSAny, JSArray, etc.) that it uses internally. This may require:
1. Adding proper export statements for js_interop types
2. Fixing extension type definitions
3. Ensuring compatibility with the latest stable Flutter/Dart SDK

## Additional Context
This issue is blocking production Android builds for applications that were previously working. The issue appeared when updating to the latest stable Flutter version (3.35.3) which was released on September 3, 2025.

## Related Issues
- This may be related to the transition from dart:html to package:web
- The issue specifically affects cross-platform builds (works on web, fails on Android/iOS)

[camera] Add framesPerSecond parameter to CameraImageStreamOptions

The CameraImageStreamOptions class in camera_platform_interface currently lacks a mechanism to specify the desired frames per second (FPS) for the camera image stream. This limitation prevents developers from controlling the frame rate of the image data received from the camera, which is crucial for various use cases requiring specific performance or resource management.

**Proposed Solution:**
Introduce a framesPerSecond parameter (e.g., an int or double) to the CameraImageStreamOptions class. This parameter would allow clients to request a specific frame rate for the image stream.

[CODE]

**Use Cases in camera packages:**

* **@camera/camera_web:**
* **Browser API Integration:** This parameter would allow camera_web to pass the desired FPS, providing more control over the streaming of image frames.
* **Video Conferencing:** For web-based video conferencing applications, controlling the frame rate can optimize bandwidth usage and improve performance in varying network conditions.

* **@camera/camera_avfoundation (iOS/macOS):**
* **AVFoundation Control:** AVCaptureDevice on iOS/macOS allows setting activeVideoMinFrameDuration and activeVideoMaxFrameDuration to control the capture frame rate. Implementing framesPerSecond would enable camera_avfoundation to configure these properties, providing fine-grained control over camera input.
* **High-Speed Video:** Applications requiring high-speed video capture or specific cinematic effects could leverage precise FPS control.

* **@camera/camera_android_camerax (Android CameraX):**
* **CameraX Use Cases:** CameraX's Preview, ImageCapture, and ImageAnalysis use cases can be configured with target frame rates. This parameter would allow camera_android_camerax to set appropriate frame rate hints for CameraX, leading to optimized camera performance and power consumption.
* **Computer Vision:** For AI/ML applications performing real-time image analysis, a consistent and controlled frame rate is essential for predictable model inference.

* **@camera/camera_windows (Windows):**
* **Windows Media Foundation:** The Windows camera APIs (e.g., via Windows Media Foundation) allow configuring frame rates for video streams. camera_windows could map framesPerSecond to the appropriate Windows API calls, ensuring proper frame rate negotiation with the camera hardware.
* **Custom Applications:** Windows applications requiring specific frame rates for recording or streaming could benefit from this control.

* **@camera/camera_android (Android Camera1/2):**
* **Legacy API Support:** Even older Android Camera1 and Camera2 APIs offer ways to set preview or capture frame rates (e.g., setPreviewFpsRange in Camera1, CONTROL_AE_TARGET_FPS_RANGE in Camera2). The framesPerSecond parameter would enable camera_android to configure these settings, supporting a wider range of Android devices and API levels.
* **Resource Management:** On resource-constrained Android devices, lowering the frame rate can reduce CPU and power consumption.

**Considerations:**

* **Platform Support:** Not all platforms or camera devices may support arbitrary frame rates. The implementation should gracefully handle unsupported requests, potentially by clamping the requested FPS to an available range or falling back to a default.
* **Negotiation:** The actual frame rate achieved might differ from the requested one due to hardware limitations or other active camera streams. The platform implementation should aim for the closest possible match.
* **Default Behavior:** If framesPerSecond is not provided, the platform should use its default or preferred frame rate.

We landed that change to resolve the issue, but a few hours later heard the Dart team's infra was broken as a result:

> flutter-analyze / flutter-analyze-trybot failures:

[CODE]

> It looks like this bot is not hermetic and it can start failing without a particular reason in Dart SDK. It is very unfortunate that it is included into CQ and these failures would block Dart SDK changes from landing.

@stereotype441 diagnosed 🙏:

> in versions of the analyzer prior to 8.2, we had some APIs that were marked as @experimental even though they weren't really experimental, and were intended to be supported for the long term. One of those APIs was the FunctionType.formalParameters getter. In [URL] (which shipped in analyzer 8.2), I removed all those bogus @experimental annotations. Later, in [URL] I added a warning to the analyzer that fires if an @experimental API gets used unintentionally. This warning is important because it unblocks new language feature development work that is currently in progress.

> The problem is that the flutter-analyze and flutter-analyze-try bots are linking the go_router_builder package to a version of the analyzer prior to 8.2, but they're analyzing that package using the bleeding edge analyzer. Which means that when go_router_builder tries to use the FunctionType.formalParameters getter, it gets flagged by the warning, even though it's actually safe (because in truth, that API isn't experimental at all; it's fully supported).

> The failure just started happening because the uses of FunctionType.formalParameters just got added to go_router_builder in [the original linked PR above].

We resolved the issue by adding ignores in [URL]
There was some confusion about which to apply where since we could not reproduce the upstream issue, which analyzer version the bot was using was not what others were using.

More info:

> The Dart team has a luci bot (flutter-analyze-try) that tries to analyze each pending SDK CL against bleeding edge flutter, and fires if that produces failures. Its purpose is to prevent us from accidentally landing changes into the dart SDK that would break the dart/flutter integration. But that bot can equally easily be broken if a change gets landed into flutter that would break the dart/flutter integation (which is what happened this time). To detect that scenario prior to landing a flutter change, we would need a bot that tries to analyze each pending flutter PR using the bleeding edge dart SDK.

flutter build ipa fails for manual signing unless a custom ExportOptions.plist is provided (Push Notifications / Sign in with Apple entitlements)

## Problem Statement

The flutter build ipa command fails during the export step when using manual code signing for iOS release or profile builds that include Push Notifications and Sign in with Apple entitlements. The archive step succeeds, but the export fails due to an incomplete ExportOptions.plist configuration.

## Reproduction Steps

1. Configure an iOS project with manual code signing:
- Set CODE_SIGN_STYLE = Manual in Xcode project settings
- Set PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER to a distribution profile name or UUID
- Configure the app with Push Notifications and Sign in with Apple entitlements

2. Run:
[CODE]

3. Result:
- ✅ Archive step completes successfully
- ❌ Export step fails:
[CODE]

## Root Cause

The provisioning profile contains the required entitlements. The failure occurs because xcodebuild -exportArchive requires a complete ExportOptions.plist with teamID and provisioningProfiles mapping when using manual signing. Flutter's default generated plist only includes method and uploadBitcode, which is insufficient.

## Current Workaround

Manually create an ExportOptions.plist with:
- method = app-store (or ad-hoc, enterprise, etc.)
- teamID = <TEAM_ID>
- signingStyle = manual
- provisioningProfiles = { "<bundle id>": "<profile UUID>" }

Then run:
[CODE]

This succeeds and produces a valid IPA.

## Impact

Developers using manual code signing for App Store distribution with Push Notifications and/or Sign in with Apple entitlements are blocked. This requires manual creation and maintenance of ExportOptions.plist files, adding friction to development workflows and CI/CD pipelines.

**Related issues:**
- #106612 - Support flutter build ipa with manual signing and provisioning profiles
- #113977 - Flutter build IPA with --export-options-plist not working

## Proposed Solution

Auto-generate a complete ExportOptions.plist for manual signing configurations when:
- CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual is detected (Release or Profile builds)
- A valid provisioning profile can be located and parsed
- Only for the main app target (not extensions/widgets)

The generated plist will respect the user's export method choice:
- Export method: whatever the user specified with --export-method (app-store, ad-hoc, enterprise, etc.)
- Team ID: from the project's DEVELOPMENT_TEAM setting
- Signing style: "manual"
- Provisioning profiles: auto-detected from system profiles

**Fallback behavior:**
- If profile lookup fails or conditions aren't met, use current behavior (simple plist)
- Automatic signing: unchanged
- Debug builds: unchanged
- Multi-target apps: unchanged

## Testing Instructions

To verify the fix:
1. Create an iOS app with CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual and Push Notifications entitlements
2. Run flutter build ipa --release --verbose
3. Verify ExportOptions.plist contains:
- teamID (from DEVELOPMENT_TEAM setting)
- signingStyle = "manual"

Remove redundant codecs on Android

This is the Android version of #144438.

Removing built-in image codecs (registered through Skia here [URL]) makes the engine fall back to trying to use Android's platform decoders for generating/decoding images. Our Android-platform-based image generator, AndroidImageGenerator [URL], is registered in AndroidShellHolder here [URL]. It is registered with a priority of -1 so that it is used as a fallback option after attempting to use the other image generators in ImageGeneratorRegisty [URL], including the built-in Skia codecs mentioned earlier.

We should consider removing the built-in codecs for image types which are supported by the fallback Android platform decoder. Removing these codecs would save on binary size.

Android supports decoding GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, and HEIF (source [URL]). So we can consider removing the built-in codecs for these image types.

#### HEIF

Flutter does not use a built-in codec for HEIF/HEIC files. These images are already using the Android platform fallback. There is no work needed for removing built-in codecs for HEIF.

#### PNG, WebP, and GIF

These image types may contain animation. Our existing AndroidImageGenerator implementation does not support animated images. It always reports a frame count [URL] of 1, and it ignores the input frame_index in its GetPixels [URL] method.

The built-in Skia decoders do support animation for these image formats (except for PNG - see next paragraph). So to remove these built-in codecs and preserve existing functionality, we need to update our AndroidImageGenerator to support animated images. This may be feasible, but is more complicated than simply removing the built-in codec and relying on our existing fallback behavior.

The built-in Skia PNG decoder that we use does not support animated PNGs. We implemented our own APNGImageGenerator [URL] which wraps the built-in Skia PNG decoder to support animation (#37247). If we want to make AndroidImageGenerator support animation, this may be a helpful example to reference.

#### JPEG

This leaves jpeg as the lowest hanging fruit for removing built-in codecs. I investigated what it would take to remove the built-in jpeg codec.

AndroidImageGenerator works by making a JNI call to FlutterJNI's decodeImage [URL] method. Currently this method only works for Android API level >= 28. It relies on Android's ImageDecoder [URL] API (used here [URL]). ImageDecoder requires API level 28+.

### API levels 24-27

We need to support Android 24+ [URL]. So we need a decoding method which doesn't depend on ImageDecoder. This can be implemented with a BitmapFactory.

[DETAILS]

### OOM on API levels 24-25 for high resolution images
From testing this implementation, it works most of the time. However, for API levels 24 and 25, I sometimes get an OOM and app crash when trying to decode high resolution images. Using a 2770x4155 image resulted in the error:
[CODE]

It is trying to allocate 46037412 bytes, which is 4 bytes per pixel for the 2770x4155 image. This causes an issue specifically for API levels 25 and below. These versions store bitmap data on the Dalvik heap. Starting with API level 26, bitmap data is stored on the native heap. (source [URL]) The Dalvik heap is much more limited than the native heap, so this causes an OOM when trying to allocate large bitmaps for API levels 25 and below.

The recommended approach [URL] for loading large bitmaps is to load a smaller scaled down version based on the size of the target UI component where the image will be displayed. The Flutter engine does not currently use information target sizing when decoding images. A potential solution may be to change the engine so that it takes target image size into account when decoding images. I do not have enough context to know what is required to do this. But I expect it would be complicated, if it is even feasible. Implementing this may be further complicated by needing to support interactions like zooming in on an image or displaying different sub-regions of a large image.

Crashing when decoding high resolution images on API levels 24-25 is a blocker. We cannot remove any of our built-in codecs until we solve this issue. The solution may be taking in target image size as described in the previous paragraph. Or it may be to simply wait until Flutter's minimum supported Android API level [URL] is bumped to 26+.

### JPEG performance testing

Putting aside the blocker of OOMs on API levels 24-25, I did some performance testing for using the Android platform codecs compared to our current built-in codec for JPEGs.

For my performance testing, I used the following test app:

[DETAILS]

With the following images:

[DETAILS]

The app shows each of the 7 images in sequence as the FAB is tapped.

I measured performance by logging the timing in three calls made in image_descriptor.cc [URL]:

registry->CreateCompatibleGenerator(immutable_buffer->data())
[DETAILS]

ImageGeneratorRegistry::CreateCompatibleGenerator is called when an ImageDescriptor is instantiated for an image. It reads header metadata from the image to determine a compatible codec, and reads some other image information (e.g. width, height, orientation) to store in the created ImageDescriptor object. This code runs on the main/UI thread, so it needs to be very quick to avoid UI jank.

ImageDescriptor::get_pixels is called to decode the image. This happens before the image can be rendered. This is expected to take longer, and it happens on a separate thread.

I ran the test app with 3 different configurations:

- Current behavior. This uses the built-in Skia codec for jpeg decoding, which uses libjpeg-turbo under the hood. This is what is launched to users.
- Removing the built-in jpeg codec. This will use the Android codec fallback, using the ImageDecoder API.
- Removing the built-in jpeg codec and forcing the Android codec fallback to use the BitmapFactory API.

For each of these configurations, I ran the app 3 times to get average timing numbers. I ran the app on a Pixel 8 device in release mode.

#### CreateCompatibleGenerator
| image | current behavior | ImageDecoder | BitmapFactory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| jpeg 1 | 0.13ms | 2.00ms | 1.08ms |
| jpeg 2 | 0.11ms | 0.69ms | 0.66ms |
| jpeg 3 | 0.14ms | 0.69ms | 1.10ms |
| jpeg 4 | 0.43ms | 1.20ms | 1.13ms |
| jpeg 5 | 0.10ms | 0.70ms | 1.33ms |
| jpeg 6 | 0.16ms | 0.95ms | 4.51ms |
| jpeg 7 | 0.25ms | 0.91ms | 0.94ms |

Both versions of the platform codec are slower than the current behavior for CreateCompatibleGenerator. The current behavior is consistently sub 0.5ms. ImageDecoder is mostly around 1ms, but jpeg 1 was 2ms. (There may be some warmup time which makes the initial jpeg a bit slower). BitmapFactory is mostly around 1ms, but jpeg 6 (notably a larger jpeg than the rest) was much slower at 4.51ms.

We strongly want CreateCompatibleGenerator to be as fast as possible, since this runs on the UI thread. If we are considering removing the jpeg codec, we must weigh the benefit of reducing the binary size with the con of slowing down these calls to CreateCompatibleGenerator.

#### get_pixels
| image | current behavior | ImageDecoder | BitmapFactory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| jpeg 1 | 14.70ms | 16.67ms | 14.90ms |
| jpeg 2 | 3.85ms | 4.19ms | 1.54ms |
| jpeg 3 | 16.91ms | 6.75ms | 13.22ms |
| jpeg 4 | 2.02ms | 2.50ms | 3.40ms |
| jpeg 5 | 14.34ms | 12.08ms | 9.51ms |
| jpeg 6 | 1257.09ms | 451.22ms | 162.31ms |
| jpeg 7 | 1.53ms | 0.16ms | 0.43ms |

Both versions of the platform codec have generally comparable get_pixels timing compared to the current behavior. The exception is with jpeg 6 (notably a larger jpeg, and notably it uses a non-sRGB color space). The current behavior is much slower to decode this image compared with the platform codecs. I dug in further to this slowdown, and believe #177805 is causing the current behavior to be extra slow.

## Summary
- Android's platform codec supports decoding GIF, JPEG, PNG, and WebP, so we can consider removing the built-in codecs for these image formats to save binary size.
- API levels 24-25 will crash with an OOM when using the platform codec with high resolution images. We should not remove the built-in codecs until this can be addressed. This may be worked around with code (may be complicated), or we may want to wait until Flutter drops support for API levels below 26.
- Using the platform codec for GIF, PNG, and WebP will not currently support animation. We could implement animation support, but will take some effort.
- Looking at using the JPEG platform codec compared to the existing built-in JPEG codec, creating ImageDecoder objects is slower. This is undesirable because it happens on the UI thread. But it may be worth considering this slowdown as a tradeoff with the benefit of reducing binary size. The actual speed of decoding is mostly comparable, but using the platform codec has the advantage that it works around #177805.

Allow SliverMainAxisGroup children to remain pinned

### Use case

This enhancement would enable powerful new composition patterns that are currently difficult or impossible to achieve cleanly with the existing Sliver API:

1. **Creating Reusable Grouped Sliver Sub-Widgets:**
* Developers often want to create a custom sliver for standalone headers that internally manages a complex layout of slivers, including a pinned widget.
* If this custom widget is used within a larger list, when the main scroll view scrolls past it, the pinned header unpins and disappears.
* With keedPinned: true, the reusable widget could manage a local pinning effect that is independent of the parent scroll position, making the pinned header behave as if it's "part of" the group's overall content block, rather than part of the main scroll container's global pinning mechanism. In the example below, **MyHeaderSliver** combine two slivers with a pinned one.

2. **Advanced NestedScrollView Integration:**
* When using a **SliverMainAxisGroup** within the **headerSliverBuilder** of a **NestedScrollView**, the current unpinning behavior means that a pinned header inside the group unpins immediately when the outer scroll view moves past the entire group.
* In some designs, it's desirable for the inner scrollable content to be able to "take over" the remaining pinned header from the outer group, or for a header to remain available for the inner scroll view *before* the inner scroll view starts scrolling (which requires the header to still be in a pinned state when the group is out of the outer viewport). This feature would provide the necessary control for more sophisticated scrolling logic between the outer and inner scrolls.

### Proposal

Introduce a mechanism, perhaps a new boolean property like keepPinned: true (or similar), on the **SliverMainAxisGroup** widget. This would effectively "lock" the pinned state of the group's children until the group's content itself is being scrolled through, irrespective of the group's position relative to the main viewport.

[Impeller] Clamp then min should just be clamp

The following 2 lines can be combined into one operation.

[URL]

[Impeller] Geometry overdraw protection can be handled by the depth compare function

(Replaces [URL]

Currently if a geometry creates a set of triangles that might overlap then it can request that we use a stencil-then-cover operation to resolve their overlapping areas before we apply the rendering operation. This adds time by requiring multiple passes to complete the operation. The stencil-then-cover processing is set up in clip_contents.cc: [URL]

Another way to prevent overdraw would be to use the fact that we already test against the depth buffer. This test is meant to clip primitives by only allowing drawing at Z values that are greater or equal (kGreaterEqual) to the current value in the depth buffer. This is used to perform complex clipping by rendering an inversion of a clip at a depth that is higher than the primitives it will clip - thus causing them to fail their Z >= depth_buffer_sample test. This test is set up in contents.cc: [URL]

Using thekGreaterEqual prevents drawing where the clip has already drawn higher (in Z) values, but does not prevent drawing over previous rendering operations that were drawn at lower (in Z) values. It also does not prevent drawing over parts of the current rendering operation when its geometry (triangular tessellation) has multiple triangles that contain the same pixels.

But, the depth comparison function kGreater would also enforce clipping for the same reason and allow drawing over prior rendering operations, again for the same reason, but in this case, the current rendering primitive could only visit the pixel once and then its own Z value put into the depth buffer would prevent the same primitive from painting that pixel a second time.

Since simply changing the depth compare function doesn't require a second pass, all cases where the Geometry objects request overdraw protection could provide that service in the normal pixel processing by simply using kGreater.

Failure to codesign iOS app due to xattr issue

## Title
**iOS Release Build Fails with Code Signing Error: "resource fork, Finder information, or similar detritus not allowed" (xattr com.apple.provenance)**

## Environment
- **macOS Version**: 15.2 (Sonoma)
- **Xcode Version**: 26.1.1 (Build 17B100)
- **Flutter Version Tested**: 3.38.5 (stable), 3.40.0 (beta), 3.35.7, 3.24.5, 3.19.6
- **Dart Version**: 3.10.4 (varies by Flutter version)
- **Target Device**: Physical iPhone (iOS 15.0+)
- **Build Configuration**: Release (ios-release)

## Description
When building Flutter iOS apps for physical device deployment, the build fails during the release_unpack_ios phase with a code signing error. The error message indicates that extended attributes (xattr) are present on the Flutter.framework binary, specifically com.apple.provenance, which Apple's code signing tool rejects.

## Error Message
[CODE]

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a standard Flutter project with iOS support
2. Configure signing credentials in Xcode (development team, provisioning profile)
3. Connect a physical iOS device
4. Run flutter build ios or use Xcode to build for device
5. Observe the build failure during code signing phase

## Root Cause Analysis
Through verbose build logging and investigation, the issue occurs because:

1. **Flutter's unpacking phase** (debug_unpack_ios/release_unpack_ios) extracts the Flutter engine binary
2. **Extended attributes are added** during extraction (specifically com.apple.provenance)
3. **Flutter itself attempts xattr removal** via xattr -r -d com.apple.FinderInfo commands, but this fails silently
4. **Xcode's code signing validation** then rejects the binary due to the presence of these xattrs
5. **The error is fatal** — code signing cannot proceed with xattrs present

## What Has Been Attempted (All Failed)
- ✅ Cleaning Flutter SDK cache and xattrs manually — xattrs are re-added during unpacking
- ✅ Podfile post_install hooks to clean xattrs — too late, unpacking occurs after pod install
- ✅ Custom Xcode build phases (pre/post signing) — file timing issues, can't intercept unpacking
- ✅ Build settings modifications — no setting controls xattr validation
- ✅ Multiple Flutter versions (3.19.6 → 3.40.0) — issue persists across all versions
- ✅ Xcode 26.1.1 (which reportedly worked in previous sessions) — still fails
- ✅ Manual xattr removal during build — doesn't persist, re-added on next invocation

## Evidence
1. **Manual xattr verification**: xattr -l on built Flutter.framework shows com.apple.provenance present
2. **Manual removal works temporarily**: xattr -d com.apple.provenance allows one build to pass
3. **Issue is not version-specific**: Tested with Flutter 3.19.6, 3.24.5, 3.35.7, 3.40.0 — all fail
4. **Verbose build logs** confirm Flutter runs xattr removal commands that fail silently

## Impact
- **Blocks iOS physical device testing** — can only use simulator
- **Affects all iOS releases** — prevents production deployment
- **Workaround-resistant** — issue occurs during Xcode unpacking phase before build configuration can intervene

## Suspected Root Cause
This appears to be a **macOS 15 (Sonoma) + Xcode 26.1+ code signing validation change** that now rejects binaries with resource fork/extended attributes that Flutter's unpacking process introduces and fails to remove.

## Questions for Flutter Team
1. Is Flutter's xattr removal in the unpacking phase working correctly on macOS 15?
2. Has Apple's code signing validation become stricter in Xcode 26.1+?
3. Is there a flag or environment variable to disable xattr addition during unpacking?
4. Should xattr removal be retried if initial attempt fails?

## Request
- **Investigate** why xattr removal fails silently during unpacking
- **Fix xattr handling** in Flutter's iOS engine unpacking phase
- **Consider** implementing robust xattr cleanup with error handling and retries

OpenTherm Gateway failed to connect

### The problem

I have an opentherm gate made according to the design from the Schelte Bron website ( [URL] I have it connected via USB to my openwrt router. On the router, I use the socat command to send a transmission from USB to the TCP port. I have Home Assistant connected via socket://IP:port to the openwrt router. Up to version core_2024.5.0 everything worked. After updating to version core_2024.5.1 (where opentherm_gw was updated to 2.2.0), my opentherm system stopped working - there was no connection to the openwrt router with socat running. I did an analysis - after updating the opentherm_gw version to 2.2.0, the integration connects to two TCP ports in parallel, which is not possible in the case of socat. Therefore, a connection error occurs. This was confirmed by the use of the Remote Access option in the otmonitor software from the Schelte website, which can be used as a relay - there is a parallel connection on two TCP ports. Network analysis using Wireshark showed this similarly - Home Assistant connects to the socat service in parallel on two TCP ports. Is there any setting in Home Assistant that forces connection to only one TCP port? Unfortunately, subsequent Home Assistant updates did not fix the error that occurred to me.

1. Set up a door sensor (or similar device) in the Tuya Smart Life app.

3. Physically open the door and observe the sensor's state change in the Tuya app (e.g., from "closed" to "open").
4. Check the state of the same sensor in Home Assistant.

The sensor state in Home Assistant should match the state shown in the Tuya app. For example, when the door is physically opened and the Tuya app shows the door as "open," Home Assistant should also display the sensor as "open."

With these parameters is reasonable that the scan could miss all 6 messages for several minutes (even hours).

### The problem

Where there is variance on RSSI/LQI per pair through the day, and where these values do not parallel other pairs, they parallel each other exactly, on all 5 links. That is, it appears LQI is just an offset of RSSI, or vice versa. The routers are not identical. 1 is a wall switch made by Ewelink, 2 are Sengled wall power switches, and 2 are Sonoff S31 Lite ZB wall power switches. Unlikely they all use the same chip, or the same stack, so this seems to be more a ZHA thing.

Make Occupancy sensor states consistent with trigger and condition strings

### The problem

All binary sensors for hazards inherit the On and Off state from the Gas binary sensor type as this matches well for Smoke, CO, Heat etc., too.

But currently this is also the case for Occupancy sensors which are not reporting a hazard at all but rather a simple state of a room. But having them inherit the same strings like smoke detectors causes quite some issues in translations where this results in the translation of the "clear" state (or "cleared" logbook entry) being changed back and forth many times as it does not fit across the board.

The inheritance is specified here:

[URL]

This results in

"off": "Clear",
"on": "Detected",

In English this is still quite obvious, but note that the trigger and condition types have already diverted from
"Has started detecting occupation" or "Is detecting occupation" etc. to the special "became occupied" or "is not occupied" instead:

[URL]

[URL]

Therefore the states above should also be decoupled from the binary Gas sensor type by either using

"off": "Not occupied",
"on": "Occupied",

making them consistent with the existing trigger and condition types.

Or by changing all occurrences of "not occupied" in above triggers and conditions to "clear", keeping that for the "off" state. Then we'd have:

"off": "Clear",
"on": "Occupied",

_Background:_
I'm reporting this because in German we had run into a major chaos because the first translation of that "Clear" state was set to "Leeren" ("to empty") which made absolutely no sense when it appeared in context. Then it was changed to "Normal" later on, but that does not fit for occupancy or motion sensors at all.

I've now changed this to "Frei" which works for everything except for motion where I set the off state to "Keine" (none).

So for occupancy here we now toggle between

"off": "Frei",
"on": "Belegt",

This also exactly matches the German translations of the triggers and conditions now (as suggested for English above) so everything is 100% consistent now.

I assume there will be similar issues in other languages, so some guidance from the English originals might help a lot here. For openings there is already separate strings which might the example to point at, too.

Venstar integration doesn't work in Celcius

### The problem

The real issue is with the Venstar Local API [URL] itself, but a workaround is probably possible in the home assistant integration itself.

If a Venstar thermostat is set to be in Celsius instead of Fahrenheit, then all of its API calls suddenly return and need temperatures in Celsius, without units.

The only API entry which has proper unit information is the /query/info [URL] one, with the tempunit entry being at 0 for Fahrenheit, and 1 for Celsius. But all the other APIs are unitless, while still modifying the meaning of their values.

In short, this means if the thermostat is set in Celsius, the current code of the integration properly retrieves the current temperature of the sensor, but then is unable to properly set the target temperature, as it is always sending Fahrenheit values, and the API is expecting Celsius. This results in the following error in home assistant when trying to set, for instance, a target temperature of 21.5C:

[IMAGE]

Two possible workarounds:

1. Cache the value of tempunit from the /query/info in order to know how to interpret and send units for the other API entries; or
2. Have a device-level setting to manually indicate the unit in which the thermostat is set.

Truly, the problem is with the API provided by Venstar, and in this case, home assistant can only. Either all values should always be in Fahrenheit, or every single API should have its unit attached to it. Is there a channel to file API bugs with Venstar?

My integration doesn't actually need it as I've already worked around it by managing bluetooth separately (which also means for example that bluetooth proxy functionality also has to be supported separately), but I think it's worth considering at least for future integration developers who might encounter the same issue.

### The problem

If a script variable uses an if-else in a template to determine whether to report true or false, the resulting value's **type** is not typed as a boolean but a string.

In contrast, if a script variable uses an if-else to determine whether to report an integer, list, or dict value, the resulting value's type is correctly typed as integer, list, or dict, respectively. Only true/false fails to be typed as boolean.

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|----------|
| 0 | Closed |
| 2 | Opening |
| 3 | Open |
| 5 | Closing |

- Greatly enhances HomeKit experience and reliability
- Avoids user confusion when status appears reversed or incorrect

SQL query considers time in HA Statistics is UTC and so brings wrong results

### The problem

Example.
I am in UTC+2. I request data at 00:00.
SQL brings me results at 02:00 - because it **assumed that since I am in UTC+2 and the HA Stats are UTC.**

WHERE
states_meta.entity_id = 'sensor.from_netz_daily'
AND last_updated_ts <= strftime('%s', 'now', '-1 day', 'start of day')
AND last_updated_ts >= strftime('%s', 'now', '-2 day', 'start of day')
ORDER BY
CAST(states.state as numeric) DESC
LIMIT
1;

As a result, for the query to bring the correct results, **the request as to mention UTC-2**

WHERE
states_meta.entity_id = 'sensor.from_netz_daily'
AND last_updated_ts <= strftime('%s', 'now', '-1 day', 'start of day', '-02:00')
AND last_updated_ts >= strftime('%s', 'now', '-2 day', 'start of day', '-02:00')
ORDER BY
CAST(states.state as numeric) DESC
LIMIT
1;

PROBLEM:
Because the Stats are not UTC but local, **any Automation can not run at the wished time....**
-> if want the data at 00:01 then the SQL would bring the results at 22:01....
- > to comply I have now to rund the automation at 02:00 to get the data at 00:00....
This means that (in my case) I have 2 hours where the results are incorrect (results from pervious day)

If I am at eg UTC+5 than I have to wait 5 HOURS to get the results at midnight

SELECT
states.state
FROM
states
INNER JOIN states_meta ON
states.metadata_id = states_meta.metadata_id
WHERE
states_meta.entity_id = 'sensor.from_netz_daily'
AND last_updated_ts <= strftime('%s', 'now', '-1 day', 'start of day', '-02:00')
AND last_updated_ts >= strftime('%s', 'now', '-2 day', 'start of day', '-02:00')
ORDER BY
CAST(states.state as numeric) DESC

go2rtc URL Encoding

### The problem

When a camera's stream_source method returns a URL containing multiple hash (#) characters for use as parameters (a common format for go2rtc's ffmpeg: source), the URL is incorrectly processed by Home Assistant's internal stream handling.

Specifically, all hash characters after the first one are URL-encoded into %23 before being passed to the stream_worker. This corrupts the source string, making it un-parsable by the go2rtc integration. The request then falls back to the default ffmpeg worker, which also fails because it doesn't understand the corrupted string, resulting in a PROTOCOL_NOT_FOUND error.

This prevents dynamically generated, complex go2rtc ffmpeg: streams from working correctly when returned from stream_source.

The string returned by a camera entity's stream_source method should be passed to the underlying stream provider (go2rtc or the default stream_worker) **verbatim**, without any URL encoding being applied to the hash/fragment components.

For example, a returned string of:
ffmpeg:rtsp://127.0.0.1:8554/test#foo=bar#baz=qux

Should be received by the worker in that exact form.

### What is happening instead?

The string is being modified. The same string from the example above is being received by the worker as:
ffmpeg:rtsp://127.0.0.1:8554/test#foo=bar%23baz=qux

This is proven by the logs below, where the custom component logs the correct string, but the stream_worker log shows the corrupted, encoded version.

Home Assistant 2025.7.x Bug: Enbrighten Zigbee switches

## Summary
Starting around July 23-24, 2025, all Enbrighten Zigbee switches in my installation began randomly turning on and off without any user input or automation triggers. The issue affects only Enbrighten devices - all other Zigbee devices work normally. **Disabling cloud exposure for Enbrighten devices completely resolved the issue**, confirming this is a cloud integration bug introduced in HA 2025.7.x.

## Home Assistant Version
- **Core:** 2025.7.3
- **Supervisor:** 2025.07.1
- **Operating System:** 2025.7.3
- **Frontend:** 20250702.3

## Problem Timeline
- **Issue started:** July 23-24, 2025 (coinciding with HA 2025.7.x update)
- **All affected devices started misbehaving on the same day**
- **Issue occurs randomly throughout the day** (when home, away, and asleep)

## Affected Devices
**All devices are Enbrighten Zigbee switches, connected via ZHA:**
- Kitchen Light (Model 43078 - Switch)
- Garage Light (Model 43078 - Switch)
- Master Bedroom Closet Light (Model 43078 - Switch)
- Butlers Pantry Light (Model 43078 - Switch)
- Fan (Model 43080 - Dimmer)

**Other Zigbee devices work normally** - only Enbrighten devices are affected.

## Symptoms
- Lights/switches randomly turn **ON** without any trigger
- Lights/switches randomly turn **OFF** without any trigger
- **No user input or automation involvement**
- Happens at completely random times (no pattern)
- Affects devices in different areas/rooms
- **Each device activates individually**, not as a group

## Evidence from Logbook
Logbook entries consistently show:
[CODE]

**Key detail: All entries show "Home Assistant Cloud" as the source**, not local automations.

### ✅ Confirmed NOT the cause:
- **Automations**: Systematically reviewed all automations - none target these devices inappropriately
- **Motion sensors**: Devices without motion sensors also affected
- **Scenes/Scripts**: No scenes or scripts call these devices
- **Mobile apps**: No location-based automations or shortcuts targeting these devices
- **External services**: No IFTTT, SmartThings, or other services connected
- **Alexa routines**: No routines control all affected devices
- **Configuration errors**: Removed misconfigured sensors, cleaned up helpers
- **Hardware issues**: All devices remain connected, other Zigbee devices work fine
- **Local network issues**: Problem persists regardless of physical location/presence

### ⚠️ What points to cloud integration bug:
- **Brand-specific issue**: Only Enbrighten devices affected
- **Simultaneous onset**: All devices started misbehaving on the same day
- **Cloud source**: Logbook consistently shows "Home Assistant Cloud" as trigger source
- **Timeline matches HA update**: Issue started around July 23-24, coinciding with 2025.7.x release

## Definitive Solution
**Disabling cloud exposure for Enbrighten devices completely stopped the random activations.**

**Steps taken:**
1. Settings → Voice assistants → Alexa → Expose tab
2. Unchecked all affected Enbrighten devices
3. **Result: Random activations immediately stopped**

This confirms the issue originates from Home Assistant's cloud integration sending spurious commands to Enbrighten devices specifically.

## Technical Environment
- **Zigbee Coordinator**: Sonoff Zigbee 3.0 USB Dongle Plus V2
- **Integration**: ZHA (Zigbee Home Automation)
- **Cloud Integration**: Home Assistant Cloud enabled with Alexa integration
- **Mobile devices**: Multiple Home Assistant mobile apps connected

## Impact Assessment
- **Severity**: High - devices activating randomly poses security/safety concerns
- **Scope**: Likely affects all users with Enbrighten Zigbee switches and HA Cloud enabled
- **Workaround available**: Disable cloud exposure (but loses voice control functionality)

## Additional Context
This appears to be a regression introduced in HA 2025.7.x that specifically affects how the cloud integration communicates with Enbrighten Zigbee devices. The consistent "triggered by action Light: Turn on" message suggests the cloud API is sending individual light service calls to these devices without proper trigger validation.

## Request for Developers
1. **Investigate cloud integration changes** in 2025.7.x that might affect Enbrighten device communication
2. **Check for spurious API calls** being sent to Zigbee devices through cloud integration
3. **Consider device-specific filtering** or validation for cloud commands
4. **Test with Enbrighten models 43078 and 43080** if available

This bug likely affects many users but may go unreported since the behavior could be mistaken for automation issues. The brand-specific nature and cloud integration involvement make this a critical issue to resolve.

## Reproduction Steps
1. Have HA 2025.7.x with Home Assistant Cloud enabled
2. Have Enbrighten Zigbee switches (43078/43080) exposed to Alexa
3. Observe random on/off activations in logbook showing "Home Assistant Cloud" source
4. Disable cloud exposure for Enbrighten devices → issue stops

---

- Installation Type: Home Assistant OS
- Zigbee Integration: ZHA
- Cloud Integration: Enabled with Alexa
- Enbrighten Models: 43078 (switches), 43080 (dimmer)

For example, a local user with read-only camera access and no network permissions can now reboot devices or change camera settings.

While hidden cameras still don’t appear in HA, the requirement to use an owner-level token creates an unnecessary attack surface.
If HA is compromised, a writable API on the UDM is exposed.

If possible, it would be safer to make the API token optional, for use cases where only limited and non-writable access is needed.

## Summary

Recent versions of the Linux kernel will automatically reset Bluetooth adapters that have somehow entered an invalid state. That's great! The way the Linux kernel exposes this to userland is by removing the previous hci device (e.g. hci0) and creating a new one (e.g. hci1). Sure, if you restart Home Assistant, then it will pick up the "new" adapter, but that's very annoying : this bug is about *not* having to restart Home Assistant.

[HomeKit Bridge] Control Center HomeKit Widgets Stay Empty (Even After Opening Home App) When Using Home Assistant HomeKit Bridge

### The problem

After updating to iOS 26, Apple introduced new Home/HomeKit widgets in the iOS Control Center.
When Home Assistant entities are exposed to Apple Home through the HomeKit integration (HomeKit Bridge), these new widgets stay completely empty, even after reboot and after opening the Home app.

Other (native) HomeKit accessories appear as expected, but all entities bridged from Home Assistant remain missing. This suggests that Apple changed the initialization or discovery behavior for HomeKit bridges, and the Home Assistant HomeKit bridge might need adjustments to support it.

Expected Behavior
- After rebooting the iPhone, Control Center should show all HomeKit entities, including those bridged from Home Assistant.
- Opening the Home app should refresh the widget view if needed.

Actual Behavior
- After reboot, the new Control Center HomeKit widget section is empty.
- Home Assistant–exposed entities do not appear at all, even after opening the Home app.
- Only native HomeKit devices (e.g., from Hue, Eve, etc.) are visible.
- No recovery occurs until (possibly) a full HomeKit bridge reload in Home Assistant.

Steps to Reproduce
- Use Home Assistant with the HomeKit integration active and paired to Apple Home.
- Expose entities (e.g., lights, switches, scenes).
- Reboot the iPhone.
- Open the Control Center → Home widget area remains empty.
- Open the Home app → still empty for Home Assistant entities.

Possible Cause / Analysis
- Apple’s new Control Center widgets might query HomeKit bridges differently (e.g., expecting immediate responses via new API calls).
- The Home Assistant HomeKit bridge may not yet respond in the expected format or timing.
- Home Assistant entities appear functional within the Home app itself, but fail to render in the new widget context.
- The issue persists even after a full Home app launch, suggesting this is not just a caching problem.

recorder: Lack of "state thrashing" protection causes DB explosion (75M+ rows) from conflicting MQTT entities

### The problem

I encountered a scenario where a configuration migration error resulted in two separate Frigate instances publishing conflicting states for the same entities to the same MQTT broker. This caused binary sensors (e.g., binary_sensor.garage_motion) to flip-flop states (ON <-> OFF) hundreds of times per minute.

Because the Recorder integration lacks rate-limiting or "thrashing protection," it faithfully recorded every single state change.

Impact: The database exploded to 38GB with 75+ Million rows in less than 5 days.

Failure of Standard Tools: The standard recorder.purge_entities service was effectively useless. Because it uses a transaction-safe "select-then-delete" loop, the estimated completion time to clear this volume of data was >20 days.

Recovery Difficulty: Recovering the system required manual, high-risk SQL intervention (stopping Core, disabling FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS/SQL_LOG_BIN as root, and running custom stored procedures) that is beyond the skill set of an average user.

Proposed Solution: Home Assistant should detect "high-frequency state thrashing" (e.g., >10 changes/sec for 60s) and temporarily disable recording for that entity, issuing a Repair issue to the user.

Home Assistant Supervisor Audio Container Breaks System HDMI Audio

## Environment
- **Hardware**: Raspberry Pi 5 (16GB) in Argon ONE V5 case
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04 Desktop ARM64
- **HA Installation**: Home Assistant Supervised (latest)
- **Audio Output**: HDMI to TV

## Problem Description

The Home Assistant Supervisor's hassio_audio container grabs exclusive access to all ALSA audio devices on the host system, completely blocking HDMI audio output for the rest of the operating system. This makes it impossible to use the Raspberry Pi as a desktop system with working audio while running Home Assistant Supervised.

### Symptoms
- After installing HA Supervised, aplay -l shows no sound cards available
- PipeWire/PulseAudio on the host cannot access HDMI audio device
- fuser -v /dev/snd/pcmC0D0p shows a root-owned PulseAudio process from the hassio_audio container
- The container runs with flags: --system --disallow-exit --exit-idle-time=-1
- This means it holds the audio device permanently and never releases it

## Expected Behavior

Home Assistant's audio features should either:
1. **Share audio devices** with the host system instead of grabbing exclusive access, OR
2. **Provide a supported way to disable the audio container** for users who don't need HA's audio features

The vast majority of HA Supervised users don't use voice assistants, TTS, or Music Assistant. For these users, the audio container serves no purpose but completely breaks system audio.

### Attempt 1: Stop the container
